title: Heat Stress & Thermoregulation
summary: Learn how the body sheds heat, adapts to hot climates and what happens when thermoregulation fails.

lessons.title: The Heat Balance Equation: Conduction to Evaporation

levels.kid:
Your body is like a little furnace that is always on. Every time you move, your muscles make heat. Running makes a lot of heat!

To stay just right, your body has to get rid of extra heat. It has four ways:
- **Touching** something cool, like sitting on a cold rock.
- **Moving air or water**, like a breeze blowing heat away.
- **Glowing heat** out into the room, the way a campfire warms your face.
- **Sweating**. When sweat dries, it carries heat away with it.

On a very hot day, the air can be warmer than you. Then sweating is your best trick. But if the air is sticky and wet, sweat can't dry well, and you heat up faster.
levels.hs:
Your body constantly makes heat through **metabolism**, the chemical reactions that keep you alive. Muscles are only about 20-25% efficient, so most of the energy they use becomes heat. To keep core temperature near 37 °C, heat gained must equal heat lost. Physiologists write this as the **heat balance equation**:

S = M − W ± R ± C ± K − E

- **S** = heat storage (positive means you're warming up)
- **M** = metabolic heat production; **W** = external work done
- **R** = **radiation**: heat traveling as infrared waves between your skin and surroundings
- **C** = **convection**: heat carried away by moving air or water
- **K** = **conduction**: heat moving by direct contact with a surface
- **E** = **evaporation**: heat lost when sweat turns into vapor

Radiation, convection and conduction depend on a temperature difference. If the air and surfaces are cooler than your skin, you lose heat; if they are hotter, you *gain* heat. Evaporation is different: it works even in hot air, as long as the air isn't too humid.

Example: a marathoner on a 35 °C sunny day gains heat from radiation and hot air, so evaporation must remove nearly all metabolic heat. If humidity is high, sweat drips off instead of evaporating, S stays positive and body temperature climbs.
levels.college:
The **heat balance equation** applies conservation of energy to the body: S = M − W ± R ± C ± K − E (some versions add respiratory heat exchange, C_res + E_res). Values are usually expressed in W·m⁻² of body surface area.

**Heat production.** Resting metabolism is roughly 80-100 W. Because mechanical efficiency is only about 20-25%, a runner producing 1000 W of metabolic power releases about 750-800 W as heat. That is enough to raise core temperature by about 1 °C every 5-8 minutes if none were lost.

**Dry (sensible) heat exchange** depends on gradients:
- **Radiation (R)**: infrared exchange proportional to the difference in surface temperatures (Stefan-Boltzmann law). Indoors at rest, it is often the largest loss route. Outdoors, sun and hot ground make it a major heat gain.
- **Convection (C)**: proportional to the skin-air temperature difference and the **convective coefficient**, which rises roughly with the square root of air velocity. Water's coefficient is far higher than air's, which is why immersion cools so fast.
- **Conduction (K)**: contact with solids; usually small, except when lying on hot or cold ground.

**Evaporative (insensible plus sweat) loss.** Vaporizing water absorbs the **latent heat of vaporization**, about 2.4 kJ per gram (≈580 kcal/L). Only evaporated sweat cools; dripped sweat is wasted. The driving force is the **water vapor pressure gradient** between wet skin (~5.6 kPa at 35 °C) and ambient air, *not* the temperature gradient.

Key consequence: once air temperature exceeds skin temperature (~35 °C), R and C reverse sign and **evaporation becomes the only route** for heat loss. High humidity shrinks the vapor pressure gradient. Clothing adds insulation and resistance to vapor flow. Both limit heat loss and push S upward.
levels.phd:
Formally, heat transfer at the skin is modeled through resistances. Dry heat loss = (T_sk − T_o)/(R_cl + 1/(f_cl·h)), where T_o is **operative temperature**, a weighted mean of air and mean radiant temperature, and h = h_r + h_c. The linearized radiative coefficient h_r is ~4.5-5 W·m⁻²·K⁻¹ near skin temperatures. Forced convective h_c scales as ≈8.3·v^0.6 in air. In water h_c is roughly 25-100 times higher, depending on flow.

Evaporation is governed by E = (P_sk,s − P_a)·w / (R_e,cl + 1/(f_cl·h_e)). Here **skin wettedness** w (0-1) is the fraction of skin covered by sweat. The **Lewis relation** links h_e ≈ 16.5·h_c (K·kPa⁻¹), so air movement boosts evaporative and convective capacity together.

Two derived quantities organize modern thinking:
- **E_req**: evaporation required for heat balance = M − W ± dry exchange.
- **E_max**: maximal evaporative capacity of the environment at w = 1.

Their ratio, w_req = E_req/E_max, predicts strain. Above roughly 0.3-0.5 sweating efficiency falls, because sweat drips rather than evaporates. When E_req > E_max the environment is **uncompensable**: core temperature rises continuously regardless of effort duration. Woodcock's permeability index and Gagge's two-node model formalized these concepts. They underpin ISO 7933 (Predicted Heat Strain).

A notable shift came from Jay and colleagues, beginning around 2011. They argued that core temperature change during exercise is set by **absolute heat production per unit mass (W·kg⁻¹)**, not by relative intensity (%VO₂max). Earlier work by Saltin and Nielsen had suggested that steady-state core temperature tracks %VO₂max. When fit and unfit subjects are matched for heat production per unit mass, core temperature changes are similar. This means comparisons matched by %VO₂max were partly confounded by body size and mass.

**Body geometry** matters. Surface-area-to-mass ratio determines heat-loss capacity relative to heat storage capacity (mass × specific heat, ~3.47 kJ·kg⁻¹·K⁻¹). This logic echoes Bergmann's and Allen's ecogeographic rules.
levels.expert:
The heat balance equation is the quantitative backbone of occupational limits, military doctrine and sports policy. Its practical pitfalls deserve attention.

**Indices versus physics.** The **WBGT** (0.7 natural wet bulb + 0.2 globe + 0.1 dry bulb outdoors) remains the regulatory standard, used by ACGIH, the US military and World Athletics. But it was built empirically and ignores metabolic rate, clothing and wind interactions. It can underestimate strain in hot-dry conditions where evaporation dominates. Rational models instead compute E_req and E_max directly. Examples are ISO 7933, Gagge's SET* and the Universal Thermal Climate Index, which is built on Fiala's multi-node model. Increasingly they are personalized with wearables that estimate core temperature from heart rate (the Buller Kalman-filter algorithm).

**Survivability limits.** Sherwood and Huber (2010) proposed a 35 °C wet-bulb ceiling based on a theoretical heat-balance limit. Empirical PSU HEAT project chamber data (Vecellio et al., 2022) found that young adults lose compensability at about 30-31 °C wet bulb in warm-humid air, and lower in hot-dry air. That finding reframes climate-health projections for older and medicated populations.

**Clinical and applied pitfalls:**
- **Encapsulating PPE**, such as bomb suits, firefighter turnouts and CBRN gear, drives E_max toward zero. Heat storage becomes almost linear in time, so work-rest cycles must be calculated rather than guessed.
- **Convective cooling coefficients** explain why **cold-water immersion** cools exertional heat stroke patients fastest (often >0.15 °C/min). It outperforms fanning or ice packs. Treatment specifics belong to the heat stroke lesson.
- **Medications shift terms in the equation.** Anticholinergics blunt sweating (reduce E). Beta-blockers and diuretics can limit skin blood flow and the volume available for sweat. Stimulants raise M.
- **Children, older adults and people with spinal cord injury** have altered surface-area ratios or reduced sweating, and these limits change their compensable range.

**Open questions** include how to validate individualized E_max in the field, and how solar load on dark skin and on clothing should be modeled. Another is whether adaptive changes in sweat efficiency alter the w_req threshold for uncompensable strain.

keyPoints: Heat storage S = M − W ± R ± C ± K − E
Muscles are ~20-25% efficient, so most energy becomes heat
Radiation, convection and conduction depend on temperature gradients
Evaporation depends on the water vapor pressure gradient, not temperature
Above ~35 °C air temperature, evaporation is the only heat-loss route
When required evaporation exceeds maximal capacity, heat stress is uncompensable

test.q: In the heat balance equation, what does a positive S indicate?
test.explain: S is heat storage. A positive value means heat gain exceeds loss, so body temperature rises.

test.q: Roughly what fraction of muscle energy use becomes heat during exercise?
test.explain: With mechanical efficiency of about 20-25%, roughly 75-80% of the energy appears as heat.

test.q: Heat carried away by moving air or water is called:
test.explain: Convection involves a moving fluid. Conduction is direct contact with a solid surface.

test.q: What drives evaporative heat loss from the skin?
choices: The speed of blood flow in muscle
test.explain: Evaporation depends on the difference in vapor pressure between wet skin and the air, which is why humidity limits it.

test.q: When air temperature is above skin temperature, which route can still remove heat?
test.explain: The dry routes reverse and add heat when the surroundings are hotter. Evaporation can still remove heat if humidity allows.

test.q: Why does sweat that drips off the body provide little cooling?
test.explain: Cooling comes from the latent heat of vaporization. Sweat that drips off never vaporizes on the skin.

test.q: At rest in a cool room, which route is often the largest source of heat loss?
test.explain: Indoors at rest, infrared radiation to cooler surroundings is typically the biggest heat-loss route.

test.q: Why does water cool the body much faster than air at the same temperature?
choices: Water raises the skin's sweat rate
Water lowers the metabolic heat rate
Water blocks infrared radiation from skin
test.explain: Water's convective heat transfer coefficient is many times higher than air's.

test.q: A runner in hot, very humid weather mainly overheats because:
choices: The vapor pressure gradient is small
test.explain: Humid air has a high vapor pressure, so sweat evaporates poorly and heat loss falls.

test.q: Heat moving by direct contact with a solid surface is called ___.
test.explain: Conduction (K) is usually small unless you lie on hot or cold ground.

test.q: Which letter in the heat balance equation stands for metabolic heat production?
test.explain: M is metabolic heat production. W is the external work done.

test.q: Vaporizing sweat absorbs the latent heat of ___, about 2.4 kJ per gram.
test.explain: This latent heat is why evaporation cools so effectively.

kidTest.q: What makes heat when you run?
kidTest.explain: Working muscles make lots of heat.

kidTest.q: How does a breeze cool you down?
kidTest.explain: Moving air carries heat away from your skin.

kidTest.q: On a very hot day, what is the body's best way to cool off?
kidTest.explain: When sweat dries, it carries heat away.

kidTest.q: Why is sticky, wet air bad for cooling?
kidTest.explain: Sweat has to dry to cool you, and wet air slows that down.

kidTest.q: Salty water from your skin that cools you: s _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Sweat cools you when it dries.

advancedTest.q: A worker's required evaporation (E_req) exceeds the environment's maximal evaporative capacity (E_max). What follows?
choices: Core temperature rises continuously as long as work continues
Sweating efficiency rises so the two match again
Core temperature reaches a higher steady plateau
Dry heat loss automatically compensates for the deficit
advancedTest.explain: When E_req exceeds E_max, the heat stress is uncompensable. No steady state exists, so heat is stored until work stops.

advancedTest.q: Jay and colleagues argued that exercise core temperature change is best predicted by:
choices: Metabolic heat production per unit body mass
Relative intensity as a percentage of VO₂max
Resting core temperature and body fat percentage
Sweat sodium concentration and total sweat volume
advancedTest.explain: Matching absolute heat production per unit body mass (W/kg) produces similar core temperature changes across fit and unfit individuals. Comparisons matched by %VO₂max are confounded by body size differences.

advancedTest.q: Why can WBGT misjudge heat strain in hot-dry conditions?
choices: It assumes that subjects are fully immersed in water
It double-counts the effect of solar radiation
It ignores metabolic rate and evaporative interactions
It uses core temperature in place of air temperature
advancedTest.explain: WBGT is empirical. It does not include metabolic rate, clothing or wind interactions, which rational models compute directly.

advancedTest.q: Why does raising air velocity improve both convective and evaporative heat loss?
choices: The Lewis relation ties h_e to h_c
Faster air lowers skin vapor pressure directly
Faster air increases mean radiant temperature
Air movement raises the skin wettedness to one
advancedTest.explain: The Lewis relation (h_e ≈ 16.5·h_c) links evaporative and convective coefficients, so increasing air speed raises both.

lessons.title: Sweating, Skin Blood Flow and Hypothalamic Control

levels.kid:
Your body has a thermostat, just like a house. It sits deep in your brain, in a small part called the **hypothalamus**. It wants you to stay close to 37 degrees Celsius.

When you run around on a hot day, your muscles make lots of heat. Sensors in your skin and your brain tell the thermostat, "It's getting warm in here!"

The thermostat then does two clever things. First, it opens up the blood vessels in your skin, so warm blood flows near the surface and loses heat. That is why your face goes pink. Second, it turns on tiny **sweat glands**. When sweat dries off your skin, it carries heat away, like a wet towel cooling you down.
levels.hs:
Your core temperature stays near 37 °C because of a control system run by the **hypothalamus**, especially an area called the **preoptic area** (POA). It works like a thermostat with a **set point**.

The system gets information from two places:
- **Central sensors**: warm-sensitive neurons in the preoptic area itself detect the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain.
- **Peripheral sensors**: nerve endings in the skin detect warmth and cold.

When you heat up, the hypothalamus triggers two main effectors through the **sympathetic nervous system**:
- **Skin blood flow rises**. Blood vessels in the skin widen (**vasodilation**), carrying heat from the core to the surface, where it can be lost to the air. In extreme heat, skin blood flow can rise from about 0.25 to 6-8 liters per minute.
- **Sweating starts**. **Eccrine sweat glands**, about 2 to 4 million of them, release watery sweat. Evaporating 1 gram of sweat removes about 2.4 kilojoules of heat. Only sweat that evaporates cools you; sweat that drips off does almost nothing.

An unusual fact: the nerves to sweat glands are sympathetic, yet they release **acetylcholine**, not noradrenaline.

Example: a cyclist on a hot day flushes red and drips with sweat. Both responses scale with how hot the core gets.
levels.college:
Thermoregulation is a negative-feedback system. The controller is the **preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus (POA)**, which integrates core temperature (sensed directly by warm-sensitive POA neurons and by visceral and spinal thermoreceptors) with skin temperature (sensed by peripheral thermoreceptors relayed through the spinal dorsal horn and the lateral parabrachial nucleus).

**Effector thresholds and sensitivity.** Each heat-loss response begins at a **threshold** core temperature and rises in proportion to further heating (its **sensitivity**, or gain). Warm skin lowers the threshold, so a hot environment starts sweating earlier. Roughly, core temperature contributes about 90% of the drive and mean skin temperature about 10%.

**Skin blood flow** is controlled differently in two kinds of skin:
- **Glabrous skin** (palms, soles, lips, ears) holds **arteriovenous anastomoses** controlled mainly by sympathetic noradrenergic vasoconstrictor tone. Warming acts by withdrawing that tone.
- **Nonglabrous (hairy) skin** has a dual supply: the same vasoconstrictor system plus an **active vasodilator system**. Active vasodilation accounts for roughly 80-90% of the cutaneous vasodilation in heat stress. It is cholinergic and uses co-transmitters, with roles for **nitric oxide**, VIP and histamine.

**Sweating.** Eccrine glands are innervated by sympathetic **cholinergic** fibers acting on **muscarinic M3 receptors**. The secretory coil produces a near-isotonic fluid. The duct then reabsorbs sodium and chloride (through ENaC and CFTR), leaving hypotonic sweat. At high sweat rates, transit is faster and less sodium is reclaimed. In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR causes salty sweat, the basis of the sweat chloride test.

**The cardiovascular trade-off.** During exercise in heat, skin and working muscle compete for cardiac output. Blood pooled in compliant skin veins, together with sweat-driven plasma loss, reduces central blood volume, stroke volume falls, and heart rate drifts upward (**cardiovascular drift**).

**Pharmacology note:** anticholinergic drugs (such as atropine, some antihistamines and tricyclics) impair sweating and raise heat risk.
levels.phd:
Modern work has replaced the single-set-point model with a picture of **multiple independent thermoeffector loops**. Romanovsky argued that each effector (sweating, cutaneous vasodilation, thermogenesis) has its own threshold and that the regulated balance point emerges from their interaction. Thresholds shift with circadian phase (about 0.5 °C), the ovarian cycle (progesterone raises luteal-phase thresholds by about 0.3-0.5 °C), fever, hydration and training.

**Neural circuitry.** Skin warm signals travel through TRPV/TRPM-expressing afferents to lamina I, then to the **lateral parabrachial nucleus**, and on to the median preoptic nucleus. Tan and colleagues (Knight lab, 2016) identified POA neurons expressing **PACAP and BDNF** that are activated by warmth and drive heat-defense behavior and vasodilation. Song and colleagues (2016) showed **TRPM2** works as an intrinsic warmth sensor in POA neurons. The POA's main output is GABAergic inhibition of thermogenic and vasoconstrictor premotor pathways in the dorsomedial hypothalamus and **rostral medullary raphe**. The descending pathway for sweating and active vasodilation is less well mapped.

**Active vasodilation mechanism.** Kellogg's microdialysis studies (from 1995) showed that botulinum toxin abolishes active vasodilation, which proves the system depends on neural release, yet atropine only modestly blunts it. Together these findings imply acetylcholine co-transmission. NOS inhibition with L-NAME cuts the response by about 30-45%. Candidate co-mediators include VIP, substance P via NK1 receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and prostanoids. The identity of the primary co-transmitter is still unresolved.

**Sweat output** equals the number of activated glands times the output per gland. Training and acclimation mostly raise the output per gland. Sweat sodium normally runs about 20-80 mmol/L, set by ductal reabsorption, which aldosterone regulates.

**Biophysics.** The heat that can be removed by evaporation depends on the gradient in water vapor pressure between skin and air. When the body needs more evaporation than the environment allows, sweat drips without cooling (**hidromeiosis** and skin wetting further reduce efficiency). Core temperature then becomes **uncompensable** and rises steadily. Sato's work established the cholinergic control of gland secretion and the role of myoepithelial cells.
levels.expert:
Clinically, these mechanisms explain why some patients are vulnerable to heat when healthy people are not.

**Pharmacologic impairment.**
- **Anticholinergic burden** (oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, tricyclics, many antipsychotics) suppresses eccrine output. **Topiramate and zonisamide** cause oligohidrosis through carbonic anhydrase inhibition, and pediatric heat-related cases are documented.
- **β-blockers** limit the rise in cardiac output that skin blood flow needs. **Diuretics** shrink plasma volume.
- **Antipsychotics** disturb central dopaminergic thermoregulation as well.
- Glycopyrronium and botulinum toxin are used therapeutically to treat **hyperhidrosis**, which shows that sweating can be blocked at a precise point.

**Neurologic disease.** **Spinal cord injury** removes sudomotor and vasomotor control below the lesion. People with tetraplegia have very little effective sweating surface and behave almost like poikilotherms during exercise in heat. **Multiple sclerosis** shows **Uhthoff's phenomenon**: small rises in core temperature worsen conduction block in demyelinated axons. **Anhidrosis** with a topographic pattern is a localizing sign. Harlequin syndrome and Horner-associated facial anhidrosis point to lesions in sympathetic pathways, and neurosurgeons meet this after **endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy** for hyperhidrosis, where **compensatory sweating** develops in most patients. A **hypothalamic lesion** (craniopharyngioma, surgery, trauma) can produce poikilothermia or central hyperthermia.

**Aging and disease.** Older adults show reduced NO-dependent active vasodilation (partly from arginase upregulation and reduced tetrahydrobiopterin) and lower output per gland. Diabetic neuropathy blunts both effectors. This physiology underlies excess deaths in heatwaves.

**Measurement pitfalls.** Laser-Doppler flux is expressed as a percentage of maximal cutaneous vascular conductance, not as absolute flow. The QSART and the thermoregulatory sweat test assess the postganglionic and the whole sudomotor pathway respectively. Regional sweat-patch sodium overestimates whole-body losses.

**Open questions.** What is the actual co-transmitter for active vasodilation? Which circuit drives sweating downstream of the POA? Do wearable sweat sensors give reliable readings? Is metabolism-based heat-loss modeling (Jay and colleagues) better than prescription by fixed temperature? Each matters for individualized heat policy.

**Pearl:** a hot, dry patient whose medication list includes anticholinergics should raise suspicion of failed sudomotor control, not just of exposure.

keyPoints: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus integrates core and skin temperature
Core temperature provides most of the drive; skin temperature shifts the thresholds
Eccrine sweat glands are sympathetic but cholinergic (muscarinic M3)
Only evaporated sweat cools; the duct reabsorbs NaCl via ENaC and CFTR
Hairy skin uses an active cholinergic vasodilator system with NO co-mediation
Anticholinergics, β-blockers and spinal cord injury impair heat loss

test.q: Which brain region acts as the main thermoregulatory controller?
test.explain: Warm-sensitive neurons in the preoptic area integrate temperature input and trigger heat-loss responses.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter stimulates eccrine sweat glands?
test.explain: Sudomotor fibers are sympathetic but cholinergic, acting on muscarinic M3 receptors. Noradrenaline is the tempting wrong answer.

test.q: Why does sweat that drips off the body provide little cooling?
choices: It lowers blood flow to the skin
It has too much sodium in it
It blocks the sweat gland ducts
test.explain: Cooling comes from the heat absorbed when water evaporates. Dripping sweat leaves the skin without evaporating, so that heat is never removed.

test.q: Roughly what share of the sweating drive comes from core temperature?
test.explain: Core temperature contributes roughly 90%, skin about 10%, although warm skin lowers the thresholds.

test.q: In hairy skin, most heat-induced vasodilation comes from:
test.explain: Active vasodilation accounts for about 80-90% of the response in nonglabrous skin. Withdrawal of vasoconstrictor tone dominates in glabrous skin.

test.q: Why is sweat normally hypotonic compared with plasma?
choices: The duct reabsorbs sodium and chloride
Sweat is filtered like urine in glomeruli
The secretory coil secretes pure water
Aldosterone adds potassium in the coil
test.explain: The coil makes near-isotonic fluid; the duct reclaims NaCl through ENaC and CFTR, leaving hypotonic sweat.

test.q: Upward drift of heart rate during prolonged exercise in heat is mainly due to:
choices: Direct heating of the sinoatrial node by blood
A steady drop in working muscle oxygen demand
Lower stroke volume from reduced blood return
Rising levels of circulating thyroid hormone
test.explain: Skin pooling and plasma loss reduce central blood volume and stroke volume, so heart rate rises to maintain cardiac output.

test.q: Which drug class is most likely to impair sweating?
test.explain: Anticholinergics block muscarinic receptors on sweat glands, reducing evaporative cooling.

test.q: Skin areas rich in arteriovenous anastomoses include:
test.explain: Glabrous skin (palms, soles, lips, ears) holds the arteriovenous anastomoses.

test.q: Sweat glands that produce watery thermoregulatory sweat are called ___ glands.
test.explain: Humans have about 2 to 4 million eccrine glands.

test.q: Defects in which chloride channel cause the salty sweat seen in cystic fibrosis?
test.explain: Defective CFTR prevents ductal chloride reabsorption, the basis of the sweat chloride test.

test.q: Widening of skin blood vessels to release heat is called ___.
test.explain: Vasodilation brings warm blood to the surface.

kidTest.q: Where is your body's thermostat?
kidTest.explain: It's in the hypothalamus, deep in the brain.

kidTest.q: Why does your face go pink when you are hot?
choices: More blood flows near the skin
Your skin gets a little sunburned
kidTest.explain: Opened skin blood vessels let heat escape.

kidTest.q: How does sweat cool you down?
choices: It blocks the sun from your skin
It dries off and takes heat away
kidTest.explain: Drying sweat carries heat off your body.

kidTest.q: About what temperature does your body try to keep?
kidTest.explain: Your body likes to stay near 37 °C.

kidTest.q: Tiny parts in your skin that make sweat are sweat g _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Sweat glands make sweat.

advancedTest.q: Botulinum toxin abolishes active cutaneous vasodilation, but atropine only modestly blunts it. The best inference is:
choices: Vasodilation is purely hormonal in origin
Muscarinic receptors are the sole mediator of the response
The response depends on circulating adrenaline
Neural release is needed, involving non-ACh co-transmitters
advancedTest.explain: Botulinum toxin blocks release of all vesicle contents, so the response is neural; resistance to atropine implies co-transmitters such as NO-linked or VIP pathways.

advancedTest.q: A tetraplegic athlete exercising in heat is at high risk mainly because:
choices: Muscle produces much more heat after the injury
Sudomotor and vasomotor outflow below the lesion is lost
Sweat glands below the lesion secrete hypertonic fluid
The preoptic area is directly damaged by the injury
advancedTest.explain: Descending sympathetic control is interrupted, leaving very little effective sweating surface or skin vasodilation.

advancedTest.q: At very high sweat rates, sweat sodium concentration rises because:
choices: Faster duct transit leaves less time for NaCl reabsorption
The secretory coil changes to hypertonic secretion
CFTR is switched off by heat
advancedTest.explain: Ductal reabsorption is limited by flow rate, so more sodium escapes when fluid moves quickly.

advancedTest.q: A worker in hot, humid air sweats heavily, yet core temperature keeps rising. The likely explanation is:
choices: Sweat glands have stopped responding to acetylcholine
Required evaporation exceeds what the vapor gradient allows
The preoptic thresholds have dropped below normal
Skin blood flow is limited by too much vasodilation
advancedTest.explain: A small skin-air vapor pressure gradient limits evaporation; dripping sweat does not cool, making heat stress uncompensable.

lessons.title: Heat Acclimatization: Plasma Volume and Sweat Changes

levels.kid:
Imagine moving to a very hot place. The first few days, you feel tired, sweaty and grumpy when you play outside. But after about one or two weeks, it gets easier. Your body has learned to handle the heat!

Here is what changes:
- Your body makes **more blood liquid**, like adding more water to a car's cooling system.
- You start **sweating sooner** and more, so you cool down faster.
- Your sweat gets **less salty**, so you keep the salt your body needs.
- Your heart does not have to beat as fast.

Scientists call this **acclimatization**. It goes away again if you stop being in the heat for a few weeks.
levels.hs:
**Heat acclimatization** is the set of changes your body makes after repeated exposure to heat, usually by exercising in hot conditions. (When it is done in a lab or heat chamber, scientists call it **acclimation**.) Most of the benefit comes within about **7 to 14 days** of daily heat exercise sessions of roughly an hour or more.

Key changes:
- **Plasma volume expands.** Plasma is the liquid part of blood. It can rise by around 10-12% within the first week, helping the heart fill and pump more blood per beat.
- **Lower heart rate** during the same exercise in the heat. The heart rate changes appear first, within about 4-5 days.
- **Lower core temperature** at rest and during exercise.
- **Earlier, greater sweating.** Sweating starts at a lower body temperature and the sweat rate rises.
- **More dilute sweat.** Sweat glands reabsorb more sodium, so you lose less salt.
- **Better comfort**, meaning exercise feels less hard.

A real example: soldiers, firefighters and athletes heading to hot competitions, such as the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, often follow heat-acclimation plans in the weeks beforehand to perform better and lower their risk of heat illness.

The adaptations **decay** if heat exposure stops. They fade over weeks, though some benefit lasts, and re-acclimatizing is usually faster the second time.
levels.college:
Repeated heat stress that raises core and skin temperature, combined with sustained sweating, triggers coordinated cardiovascular, sweat-gland and cellular adaptations.

**Time course** (typical with daily exposures):
- Days 3-6: plasma volume expansion and reduced exercise heart rate.
- Days 5-14: lower core temperature, increased sweat rate, reduced sweat sodium.
- Roughly 75-80% of adaptation occurs in the first week.

**Plasma volume (PV) expansion.** PV increases by about 4-15%, driven by:
- **Aldosterone**, which increases renal sodium retention and expands the extracellular fluid.
- **Increased plasma albumin** (more synthesis, less loss), raising oncotic pressure and holding fluid in the vessels.
- Larger PV raises central blood volume, preserving **stroke volume** while skin blood flow competes with muscle for cardiac output. Heart rate therefore falls for a given workload.
- PV expansion is partly transient and may return toward baseline with prolonged acclimatization, even as other adaptations persist.

**Sweat adaptations.**
- Lower core-temperature **threshold** for sweating onset and greater sensitivity (more sweat per degree of temperature rise).
- Higher maximal sweat rate, with better distribution toward the limbs.
- Aldosterone acts on the eccrine duct (ENaC, Na+/K+-ATPase), boosting Na+ and Cl- reabsorption, so sweat [Na+] can fall by about half.
- Consequence: fluid needs **increase**, not decrease. Acclimatized people sweat more and still need to drink.

**Other changes**: lower resting core temperature, improved skin blood flow at a lower threshold, reduced glycogen use, and improved thermal comfort.

**Protocols**: Isothermic or controlled-hyperthermia methods clamp core temperature near 38.5 °C. They induce adaptation more consistently than fixed-workload protocols. Passive methods, such as post-exercise hot baths or sauna, also work.
levels.phd:
Heat acclimation is a phenotype built from overlapping signals: elevated core temperature, high skin temperature, sustained sweating and the hypovolemic stimulus of fluid loss. The **thermal impulse**, meaning the magnitude and duration of core temperature elevation, best predicts adaptation, which is why controlled-hyperthermia protocols outperform fixed-intensity ones.

**Volume regulation.** Early PV expansion reflects intravascular protein accretion. Senay's classic work showed albumin moves into the vascular space early in acclimation. Each gram of retained albumin binds about 14-15 mL of water. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, activated by repeated sweating and natriuresis, expands total extracellular volume. Hypohydration during sessions may amplify this stimulus, though permissive dehydration protocols show inconsistent added benefit. PV gains peak around one week and partly regress over 2-3 weeks of continued exposure. Cardiovascular stability is then maintained by other means, including improved venous tone and cutaneous vasomotor control.

**Sweat gland plasticity.** Acclimation shifts the sudomotor threshold leftward and raises its gain. Eccrine glands hypertrophy and become more cholinergically sensitive. Ductal NaCl reabsorption rises via mineralocorticoid-driven upregulation of ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase. A higher sweat rate itself raises sweat [Na+], because ductal reabsorption saturates at high flow, so comparisons must be flow-matched. **Hidromeiosis**, the decline of sweating on persistently wet skin, is reduced after acclimation in some studies.

**Cellular thermotolerance.** Repeated heat induces heat shock proteins, notably **HSP70 and HSP90**, via HSF1. These confer acquired cytoprotection, which Horowitz framed as heat acclimation-mediated cross-tolerance to hypoxia and ischemia. Proposed epigenetic "memory", such as histone modification at HSP loci, may explain faster re-induction.

**Controversies.** It remains debated whether heat acclimation improves performance in temperate conditions. Lorenzo et al. (2010) reported VO2max gains in cool environments attributed to PV expansion, but later controlled trials, such as Keiser et al. (2015), found that plasma volume expansion alone did not explain them and replication was mixed. Decay also varies: roughly 2.5% of adaptation is lost per day without heat, with heart-rate adaptations retained better than sweat ones in some datasets.
levels.expert:
Applied heat acclimation is now standard in military, occupational and elite-sport planning. Expert consensus statements (e.g., Racinais et al., 2015, British Journal of Sports Medicine) recommend 1-2 weeks of daily sessions of at least 60 minutes that raise core temperature, finishing shortly before the hot event.

**Practical protocol design.**
- **Short-term** (under 7 days) and **long-term** (over 14 days) protocols produce different phenotypes. Sweat-sodium conservation and maximal sweat rate keep improving past one week.
- **Re-acclimation** after decay is faster. Intermittent "top-up" sessions every few days help preserve adaptations during tapering or travel.
- **Post-exercise hot-water immersion** (Zurawlew et al.) gives meaningful adaptation with little extra training load, which suits athletes who cannot change their outdoor environment.
- **Humidity matters**. Humid heat emphasizes sweat efficiency and skin wettedness tolerance; adapting in dry heat transfers imperfectly.

**Monitoring.** Useful markers include exercise heart rate, rectal or gastrointestinal-pill core temperature, sweat rate from body-mass change, and PV estimated by the Dill-Costill method from hemoglobin and hematocrit. Pitfall: hemodilution from PV expansion lowers hemoglobin concentration. This can mimic anemia or confound hematologic athlete-passport readings, so testers must interpret it with context.

**Clinical caveats.** Acclimatization lowers but does not abolish heat illness risk. Higher sweat rates raise fluid demand. Medications that impair thermoregulation can blunt adaptation or its protective effect. These include anticholinergics (reduced sweating), beta-blockers (reduced cardiac reserve and skin blood flow), diuretics (volume loss) and stimulants (heat production). Older adults, children and people with spinal cord injury or cystic fibrosis show altered sweat or volume responses. Return-to-heat plans after illness should re-acclimate progressively.

**Open questions.**
- Do individual "responders" differ genetically, for example through HSP polymorphisms?
- Can cross-adaptation with altitude be exploited, through shared HIF-1 and HSP pathways, or do combined stresses interfere?
- What is the true mechanistic contribution of epigenetic heat memory in humans?
- How should climate change reshape occupational acclimatization standards, such as OSHA-style ramp-up schedules for new workers? Many workplace heat deaths occur in the first days on the job.

keyPoints: Heat acclimatization develops over about 7-14 days of repeated heat exposure
Plasma volume expands early via aldosterone and albumin, stabilizing stroke volume
Heart rate and core temperature fall for the same work in the heat
Sweating starts earlier, is greater and contains less sodium
Heat shock proteins add cellular thermotolerance
Adaptations decay without heat but return faster on re-exposure

Lower skin temperature at high flow reduces sodium secretion

Keep the thermal impulse high as fitness to heat improves

lessons.title: Exertional Heat Stroke: From Hyperthermia to Organ Failure

levels.kid:
Your body is like a car engine. When you run hard, your muscles make lots of heat. Usually your body cools itself by sweating and sending warm blood to your skin.

But on a very hot, sticky day, if you push too hard, the heat can pile up faster than your body can get rid of it. When the inside of your body gets far too hot, the brain stops working properly. A person might get confused, act strangely or pass out. This is called **heat stroke**, and it is an emergency.

The best fix is to cool the person down fast, like putting them in a tub of ice water, while someone calls for help. Cooling first, quickly, saves lives.
levels.hs:
**Exertional heat stroke (EHS)** happens when hard exercise makes the body produce heat faster than it can lose it, so core temperature climbs dangerously high. It is defined by two things together:
- **Hyperthermia**: core body temperature usually above about **40 °C (104 °F)**.
- **Central nervous system dysfunction**: confusion, odd behavior, collapse, seizures or coma.

The brain problem is the key sign. A tired, sweaty athlete who is thinking clearly may have **heat exhaustion**, which is milder. An athlete who is confused or acting "not themselves" should be treated as having heat stroke until proven otherwise. Many people with EHS are still sweating, so dry skin is not required.

Why is it dangerous? Very high temperatures damage cells directly. The gut lining becomes leaky, blood clotting goes haywire, muscles break down, and the kidneys and liver can fail.

A real example: in American football, heat stroke has killed players during hot preseason practices in full pads, often in the first days of training before their bodies adapted to heat.

The rule is **"cool first, transport second."** Cold-water immersion (putting the body in ice water up to the neck) cools fastest. When cooling begins within about 30 minutes, survival approaches 100%. Temperature must be measured rectally, because mouth, ear or forehead readings are unreliable after exercise.
levels.college:
Exertional heat stroke arises when metabolic heat production during exercise (which can rise 10 to 20 times above resting) exceeds heat loss. Hot, humid conditions limit evaporation, and heavy clothing or equipment adds insulation. Core temperature rises past about 40 °C, and central nervous system dysfunction appears.

**Risk factors**
- Lack of heat acclimatization, poor fitness, high body mass
- High wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), which combines heat, humidity and radiant load
- Dehydration, recent illness or fever, sleep loss
- Motivation to push through warning signs (soldiers, athletes)
- Drugs that impair heat loss or raise heat production, such as anticholinergics (reduce sweating) and stimulants such as amphetamines

**From heat to organ damage**
- **Direct cytotoxicity**: proteins denature and membranes destabilize; damage depends on both temperature and time spent hot.
- **Gut ischemia and endotoxemia**: blood is diverted from the gut to skin and muscle, so the intestinal barrier leaks and bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) enters the circulation, triggering a cytokine-driven inflammatory response similar to sepsis.
- **Coagulopathy**: endothelial injury can progress to **disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)**.
- **Rhabdomyolysis**: damaged muscle releases myoglobin, potassium and creatine kinase, risking **acute kidney injury** and dangerous arrhythmias.
- **Liver injury**: transaminases often peak 24 to 72 hours after collapse.
- **Brain**: cerebellar Purkinje cells are especially vulnerable to heat, so lasting ataxia can occur.

**Classic versus exertional**: classic heat stroke affects elderly or chronically ill people during heat waves, often with dry skin. EHS strikes young, healthy people who are exercising, and they are often still sweating.

**Treatment**: cold-water immersion cools at roughly 0.15 to 0.35 °C per minute. Stop active cooling at about 38.6 to 39 °C to avoid overshooting into hypothermia. Antipyretics such as acetaminophen do not work, because the hypothalamic set point is not raised.
levels.phd:
EHS is best conceptualized as a **thermal dose** problem: injury scales with the magnitude and duration of hyperthermia, analogous to cumulative equivalent minutes in hyperthermia oncology. Cellular injury accelerates above about 41 to 42 °C. Mechanisms include protein unfolding, cytoskeletal collapse, mitochondrial uncoupling and loss of membrane integrity. Clinical outcome tracks the **time above roughly 40.5 °C** better than the peak temperature, which explains why rapid cooling nearly abolishes mortality.

**The endotoxin hypothesis.** Splanchnic blood flow falls sharply during exertional heat stress. Tight-junction proteins (occludin, ZO-1) are disrupted, and LPS translocates into portal blood. Bouchama and Knochel's 2002 *NEJM* review framed heat stroke as a systemic inflammatory response. Supporting evidence includes elevated IL-6, TNF-α and IL-1β, and studies in primates showing that anti-LPS strategies improved survival. Plasma LPS rises are inconsistent in humans, however, and the relative weight of endotoxemia versus direct heat injury remains debated. Damage-associated molecular patterns (HMGB1, histones) released from heat-damaged cells may drive the same Toll-like receptor signaling without bacteria.

**Heat shock proteins.** HSP70 and HSP90, induced through HSF1, refold damaged proteins and dampen NF-κB signaling. Acclimatization and training raise basal HSP levels, an effect called acquired thermotolerance, which is partly why unfit, unacclimatized people are vulnerable. Aging blunts the HSP response.

**Coagulation.** Heat activates the endothelium, causing tissue factor expression and early hyperfibrinolysis. This can progress to consumptive DIC and is a major predictor of death.

**Genetic susceptibility.** Some EHS survivors carry variants in **RYR1**, the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor implicated in malignant hyperthermia. In mouse models (RYR1 Y524S), heat or exertion triggers uncontrolled sarcoplasmic Ca²⁺ leak and hypermetabolism. The overlap is incomplete, and most EHS patients have no identified variant.

**Thermoregulatory failure.** The leading view is that EHS reflects overwhelming heat production plus circulatory limits, as falling cardiac output forces a choice between skin and muscle perfusion, rather than a true failure of the hypothalamic thermostat.
levels.expert:
Field management determines outcome more than anything done in hospital. Key operational points:
- **Diagnosis**: rectal (or esophageal) temperature is mandatory. Oral, tympanic, temporal-artery and axillary readings underestimate core temperature after exertion. A lucid interval can mislead; any mental status change in a hot, exerting athlete warrants immediate immersion.
- **Cool first, transport second**: if cold-water immersion is available on site, cool before transfer. Delays from ambulance transfer to an emergency department, where immersion is rarely possible, are a classic avoidable death. Tarp-assisted cooling and rotating ice-water towels are acceptable alternatives. Evaporative misting with fans is slower.
- **Endpoint**: remove the patient from the water at about 38.6 to 39 °C, then monitor for rebound.

**Hospital phase.** Watch for hyperkalemia and arrhythmia, hypoglycemia, rhabdomyolysis (CK can rise to tens of thousands of units per liter), AKI that may need renal replacement, DIC and fulminant hepatic failure. Liver transplant for heat-stroke liver failure is rare and controversial because outcomes are poor. Dantrolene showed no convincing benefit in non-MH heat stroke trials. Endotoxin-, cytokine- and coagulation-targeted therapies such as activated protein C and IL-1 blockade remain unproven in humans.

**Differential pitfalls.** Exertional collapse can also be exertional sickling in sickle-cell trait, cardiac arrest, exercise-associated hyponatremia, hypoglycemia or a serotonergic or sympathomimetic toxidrome. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia can mimic heat stroke but need different, specific management.

**Return to play.** Military and sports guidelines (for example ACSM 2023, US Army) use graded re-exposure once labs normalize. Heat tolerance testing, such as the Israeli Defense Forces protocol of walking in about 40 °C heat while tracking rectal temperature and heart rate, is used, though its predictive validity is debated.

**Open questions** include biomarkers that predict organ failure or recurrence, how long immune and thermoregulatory vulnerability lasts after EHS, and long-term cardiovascular and renal risk. Danish and Taiwanese cohort data suggest elevated long-term mortality.

For a neurosurgery-minded student: cerebellar atrophy after EHS, seen on MRI and causing persistent dysarthria and ataxia, is a clear example of how sensitive Purkinje cells are to heat.

keyPoints: Exertional heat stroke = core temp above about 40 °C plus CNS dysfunction
Altered mental status is the key sign; sweating may persist
Injury scales with thermal dose: how hot and for how long
Gut leak, inflammation, DIC, rhabdomyolysis and liver/kidney failure follow
Rectal temperature is the reliable measurement
Cool first (cold-water immersion), transport second

test.explain: Rectal (or esophageal) temperature is accurate. The other methods underestimate core temperature after exertion.

Ice packs placed on the forehead

test.q: Why do antipyretics like acetaminophen fail in heat stroke?

They are destroyed by high temperatures
The gut absorbs them poorly in the heat
test.explain: Fever involves a raised set point, which antipyretics lower. In heat stroke, heat production simply overwhelms heat loss.

It releases myoglobin into the blood

test.explain: Damaged muscle releases myoglobin, which can cause acute kidney injury, along with potassium and creatine kinase.

choices: Elderly people during a heat wave
test.explain: Classic heat stroke affects elderly or chronically ill people during heat waves. EHS affects young, healthy people who are exercising.

test.explain: Stopping at about 38.6 to 39 °C avoids overshooting into hypothermia.

test.q: Which brain cells are especially vulnerable to heat injury?
test.explain: Purkinje cells are highly heat-sensitive, so survivors can have lasting ataxia.

test.q: The guiding rule of field care is "cool first, ___ second."
test.explain: Cooling on site before transfer prevents deadly delays.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the widespread clotting disorder that can complicate heat stroke?
test.explain: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a major predictor of death in heat stroke.

test.explain: Many people with EHS keep sweating, so dry skin is not a requirement for diagnosis.

kidTest.q: What makes most of the heat when you run?
kidTest.explain: Working muscles make lots of heat.

kidTest.q: What is a warning sign of heat stroke?
kidTest.explain: When the brain gets too hot, a person can become confused or pass out.

kidTest.q: What is the best way to help someone with heat stroke?
kidTest.explain: Cooling fast in ice water saves lives.

kidTest.q: What kind of day makes heat stroke more likely?
kidTest.explain: On hot, sticky days, sweat cannot dry well and cool you down.

kidTest.q: Your body cools by making s _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Sweat cools the skin as it dries.

advancedTest.q: Outcomes in EHS track time above about 40.5 °C better than peak temperature. The best inference is that:
choices: Injury reflects cumulative thermal dose, so cooling speed matters most
Endotoxemia, rather than heat itself, explains most of the organ damage
Peak temperature readings are unreliable in the field and should be ignored
Brain damage starts once core temperature passes a fixed 42 °C threshold
advancedTest.explain: Injury scales with both magnitude and duration of heat, so rapid cooling nearly abolishes mortality.

advancedTest.q: Plasma LPS rises are inconsistent in human EHS, yet inflammation is marked. Which explanation fits the lesson best?
choices: Cytokines in EHS come mainly from sweat glands

Acetaminophen blocks LPS detection in patients
Heat shock proteins directly secrete IL-6 into plasma
advancedTest.explain: Damage-associated molecular patterns released by heat-damaged cells can drive TLR signaling without bacteria.

advancedTest.q: Why might unacclimatized, unfit individuals be more vulnerable at the cellular level?
choices: Their hypothalamic set point is chronically raised
They have lower basal heat shock protein levels
Their gut produces less endotoxin at baseline
They carry RYR1 variants much more frequently
advancedTest.explain: Training and acclimatization raise basal HSP70 and HSP90 levels (acquired thermotolerance), which limits protein damage.

advancedTest.q: An athlete is transported unimmersed to an ED 40 minutes away despite an ice tub on site. The main error is:
choices: Skipping a heat tolerance test before the transfer
Extending time hyperthermic, raising the thermal dose
Failing to give dantrolene before transport begins
Using rectal rather than oral temperature monitoring
advancedTest.explain: Cooling should precede transport. Delay extends the thermal dose, and immersion is rarely possible in an ED.

lessons.title: Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia

levels.kid:
Your blood is a little bit salty, like a very weak soup. That salt, called **sodium**, helps your brain and muscles work.

When you run a long race, you sweat out water and some salt. Drinking is good. But some people drink much more water than they lose. Then the salt in their blood gets too watered down, like soup with too much water added.

This is called **hyponatremia**. It can make you feel sick, confused or puffy. In bad cases the brain swells, which is very dangerous.

The smart rule is simple: drink when you feel thirsty. Your body's thirst signal is a good guide. You don't need to force down extra water.
levels.hs:
**Exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH)** means a low blood sodium level during or up to 24 hours after exercise. Doctors define it as a serum sodium below **135 mmol/L**. Normal is about 135 to 145.

**Sodium** is the main salt in the fluid outside your cells. It controls where water goes. If sodium in the blood drops, water moves by **osmosis** into cells, making them swell. Most organs cope, but the brain is trapped inside the skull, so swelling there raises pressure.

The main cause is **drinking more fluid than you lose** through sweat and urine. A second factor is a hormone called **ADH** (antidiuretic hormone, or vasopressin). It tells the kidneys to hold onto water. During long exercise, ADH can stay high even when you have plenty of water, so the extra fluid isn't peed out.

Risk factors include:
- Long events like marathons, ultramarathons and triathlons
- Slower finishers, who have more time to drink
- Weight gain during the race, a strong warning sign

Symptoms range from nausea, bloating and headache to confusion, seizures and coma.

A real example: in the 2002 Boston Marathon, a study of 488 runners found 13% had hyponatremia, and 0.6% had critical levels. The best prevention is **drinking to thirst**.
levels.college:
EAH is defined as serum or plasma [Na⁺] below 135 mmol/L occurring during or within 24 hours of prolonged physical activity. It differs from the dehydration-related problems athletes are usually warned about. Most cases are **dilutional**: total body water rises relative to total exchangeable sodium.

**Pathophysiology** combines three factors:
- **Excess fluid intake** beyond sweat, respiratory and renal losses. This is the dominant cause. Body weight gain during an event strongly predicts low sodium.
- **Non-osmotic AVP (arginine vasopressin) secretion.** Exercise stimuli such as nausea, pain, stress, hypoglycemia, raised core temperature and interleukin-6 can drive AVP release despite low plasma osmolality. This mimics **SIAD** (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis) and stops the kidneys excreting free water.
- **Sodium losses and failure to mobilize sodium stores.** Sweat sodium losses add to the problem but rarely cause severe EAH alone.

**Consequences.** Lower plasma osmolality drives water into cells. In the brain this causes **cerebral edema**. Rising intracranial pressure can produce headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures and coma. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema can also occur, worsening hypoxemia and brain swelling.

**Risk factors**: event longer than about 4 hours, slow pace, low body mass, abundant drink stations, NSAID use and inexperience. Women were overrepresented in early studies, largely because of smaller size and slower times.

**Diagnosis** needs a point-of-care sodium measurement, since symptoms overlap with exertional heat stroke, hypoglycemia and exhaustion.

**Management principles**: stop all hypotonic fluids. Mild, asymptomatic cases can be watched with fluid restriction until urination begins. Symptomatic patients get **hypertonic (3%) saline** given as a bolus to quickly shrink brain swelling. Giving isotonic saline or more water to a confused runner presumed "dehydrated" can be fatal.
levels.phd:
EAH is a disorder of water balance more than of sodium balance. Plasma [Na⁺] approximates (total exchangeable Na⁺ + K⁺) / total body water, per the **Edelman equation**. Most severe cases show expanded total body water from intake exceeding losses, with AVP-mediated water retention.

**Historical arc.** Noakes described hyponatremic encephalopathy in Comrades Marathon runners in 1985, challenging dogma that heat-trained athletes should drink maximally. Guidance encouraging drinking "as much as tolerable" coincided with rising EAH incidence. Almond et al. (NEJM 2005) studied 488 Boston Marathon finishers: 13% had [Na⁺] ≤135 and 0.6% were ≤120. The strongest predictors were weight gain, race time over 4 hours, and BMI extremes. Sex was not significant after adjustment.

**Non-osmotic AVP.** Hope et al. and Siegel's group measured plasma AVP or **copeptin** (a stable AVP surrogate) and found it inappropriately elevated in hyponatremic runners. Candidate drivers include:
- Splanchnic hypoperfusion and reduced effective volume sensed by baroreceptors
- Nausea and vomiting, which are among the most potent AVP stimuli
- IL-6 from contracting muscle
- NSAIDs, which inhibit renal prostaglandins and enhance the action of AVP at collecting-duct **V2 receptors**

**The osmotically inactive sodium pool.** Some runners develop hyponatremia with smaller water excess than predicted. Others overdrink yet stay normonatremic. This suggests variable mobilization or sequestration of sodium in bone and skin glycosaminoglycan stores, as proposed by Titze's work on interstitial sodium. Whether this explains individual susceptibility remains contested.

**Cerebral adaptation.** Brain cells adapt over 24 to 48 hours by extruding osmolytes (K⁺, glutamate, taurine, myo-inositol). EAH develops over hours, too fast for this adaptation. Acute EAH therefore carries high edema risk. The upside is that rapid correction carries low risk of **osmotic demyelination syndrome**, unlike chronic hyponatremia.

**Controversy.** Industry-funded hydration science and the "stay ahead of thirst" message are debated. The 2015 International EAH Consensus Conference (Hew-Butler et al.) endorsed drinking to thirst as the primary prevention strategy.
levels.expert:
In the medical tent, EAH is a diagnosis you either measure or miss. A collapsed endurance athlete has a short differential: exercise-associated collapse (postural hypotension after stopping), exertional heat stroke, hypoglycemia, cardiac events and EAH. Rectal temperature and point-of-care sodium should come early, because two of these have opposite fluid treatments.

Clinical pearls from the 2015 consensus and field experience:
- **Encephalopathic EAH is treated before transfer.** The consensus protocol uses a fixed-volume bolus of 3% saline, repeated if neurologic signs persist, rather than a weight-based calculation. A small rise in [Na⁺] of about 4 to 5 mmol/L is usually enough to reverse herniation physiology.
- **Empiric hypertonic saline is reasonable** in a clearly encephalopathic runner with suspected EAH when no analyzer is available, because the risk of harm is low in acute hyponatremia.
- **Never reflexively give isotonic IV fluid.** Normal saline in a patient with high AVP can be retained as free water once the sodium is excreted in concentrated urine, a process called **desalination**. This can further lower [Na⁺].
- **Beware delayed presentation.** Fluid pooled in the gut can be absorbed after the finish, so sodium can fall in the hours after a race. Discharge criteria should include confirmed urination and stable mental status.
- **Watch for overcorrection** once AVP falls and a water diuresis begins. This matters most if hyponatremia started before the race, for example in athletes on thiazides or SSRIs, or with other chronic causes.

**Beyond running**: EAH occurs in military training, hiking (notably Grand Canyon rescues), ironman triathlons, long-distance swimming and even yoga in heated rooms. Military policies capping hourly water intake were introduced after fatal cases in trainees.

**Open questions**:
- Can salt capsules or sodium-rich drinks prevent EAH? Trials suggest they do little if overdrinking continues.
- Do genetic variants in AVP regulation or aquaporin-2 predict who is susceptible?
- Can wearable sweat-sodium sensors guide individual fluid plans?
- How should event organizers space aid stations to discourage overdrinking without risking dehydration in the heat?

For future neurosurgeons, EAH is a model of acute cerebral edema in which the cause is measurable and rapidly reversible.

keyPoints: EAH is serum sodium below 135 mmol/L during or within 24 h of exercise
Main cause is drinking more fluid than is lost
Non-osmotic vasopressin (AVP) release stops free-water excretion
Low sodium drives water into brain cells, causing cerebral edema
Symptomatic EAH is treated with hypertonic (3%) saline boluses, not isotonic fluid
Drinking to thirst is the main prevention strategy

test.q: Exercise-associated hyponatremia is defined as a serum sodium below:
test.explain: EAH is a sodium below 135 mmol/L. Values of 120 or less are severe, but they are not the cutoff.

test.q: What is the main cause of most EAH cases?
choices: Too little fluid during the race
test.explain: Most EAH is dilutional, caused by fluid intake exceeding losses. Sweat sodium loss contributes but rarely causes severe EAH alone.

test.q: Why is the brain especially endangered when blood sodium falls?
choices: Blood flow to the brain stops at once
Swelling occurs inside the rigid skull
Brain cells shrink and tear vessels
test.explain: Water moves into cells by osmosis. The skull limits expansion, so brain swelling raises intracranial pressure.

test.q: Which finding during a marathon most strongly predicts hyponatremia?
test.explain: Gaining weight shows that fluid intake exceeded losses, the core cause of EAH.

test.q: Non-osmotic vasopressin release during exercise causes the kidneys to:
test.explain: AVP acts on the collecting duct to keep water. When it stays high despite low osmolality, extra fluid is not excreted.

test.q: Which runner is at highest risk of EAH?
choices: Slow runner drinking at each stop
test.explain: Long race times and frequent drinking give more opportunity to overload fluid.

test.q: A confused marathoner has a low measured sodium. The best first treatment is:
test.explain: Hypertonic saline quickly raises sodium and reduces brain swelling. More hypotonic or isotonic fluid can worsen EAH.

test.q: Which drug class can worsen EAH by enhancing vasopressin's action in the kidney?
test.explain: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandins, which boosts AVP's water-retaining effect at V2 receptors.

test.q: The recommended primary prevention strategy for EAH is:
test.explain: The 2015 consensus endorsed drinking to thirst. Salt capsules do little if overdrinking continues.

test.q: Water moves into cells when blood sodium falls, a process called ___.
test.explain: Osmosis moves water toward the more concentrated side, here into the cells.

test.q: What abbreviation names the hormone that tells the kidneys to hold onto water?
test.explain: ADH, also called arginine vasopressin (AVP), promotes water retention.

test.q: Swelling of the brain in severe EAH is called cerebral ___.
test.explain: Cerebral edema raises intracranial pressure and can cause seizures and coma.

kidTest.q: What salt in your blood gets watered down in hyponatremia?
kidTest.explain: Sodium is the salt that gets too diluted.

kidTest.q: What usually causes this problem in long races?
choices: Running too fast at the start
kidTest.explain: Too much water waters down the salt in your blood.

kidTest.q: Which body part is in the most danger when it swells?
kidTest.explain: The brain is inside the hard skull, so swelling there is dangerous.

kidTest.q: What is the smart rule for drinking during a race?
choices: Drink at each stop you pass
kidTest.explain: Thirst is a good guide for how much to drink.

kidTest.q: Drink when you feel t _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Your thirst signal tells you when your body needs water.

advancedTest.q: Why is rapid correction of EAH safer than rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia?
choices: Exercise strengthens myelin against osmotic stress
Hypertonic saline does not cross into brain tissue
Athletes have unusually high baseline sodium stores
Brain cells have not yet shed osmolytes in hours
advancedTest.explain: Osmolyte extrusion takes 24 to 48 hours. Acute EAH lacks this adaptation, so quick correction carries little risk of osmotic demyelination.

advancedTest.q: Isotonic saline can lower sodium further in EAH because:
choices: It blocks vasopressin at V2 receptors
It contains less sodium than plasma does
It shifts potassium out of muscle cells
Its sodium is excreted while its water is kept
advancedTest.explain: With high AVP, kidneys excrete the sodium in concentrated urine and keep the water, a process called desalination.

advancedTest.q: Almond's Boston study found sex was not significant after adjustment. The best interpretation is:
choices: Female hormones directly protect against EAH
Sweat sodium loss differs mainly by sex
Body size and race time explain the sex effect
Men overdrink more than women at stations
advancedTest.explain: Higher crude rates in women reflected smaller body mass and slower times, not sex itself.

advancedTest.q: Two runners drink equal excess water; only one becomes hyponatremic. A proposed explanation is:
choices: Different core temperatures at the finish
Different rates of sweat gland hypertrophy
Unequal stomach emptying of sports drinks
Variable sodium release from skin and bone stores
advancedTest.explain: Varying mobilization of osmotically inactive sodium stores may explain individual susceptibility, though this remains contested.
